concept.body: Isosceles angle arithmetic: apex + 2(base angle) = 180. Given the apex, each base angle = (180 − apex)/2. Given a base angle, apex = 180 − 2(base angle). The two BASE angles are the equal pair; the apex sits between the legs and can differ.

explanationVariants: Subtract the apex, halve the rest: (180 − 80)/2 = 50°.

widget.prompt: An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 80°. What is each base angle, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 100 = 180 − 80 is the two base angles COMBINED. Each is half: 100 ÷ 2 = 50°.
80° is the apex. Base angles are (180 − 80)/2 = 50° each.

steps.body: An **isosceles** triangle has two equal sides — the **legs** — and the angles opposite them, the **base angles**, turn out equal too. This is the Base Angles Theorem: equal legs force equal base angles. It's not obvious from looking; it earns its certainty from a congruence proof.

widget.prompt: The legs are locked equal at 7. Drag the apex angle toward 40° and watch the two base angles — can you make them disagree?
widget.constraintFeedback: You released the lock — the legs are no longer equal, so the base angles are reading a DIFFERENT triangle than the one the theorem is about. Lock them again.
widget.successFeedback: 70° each — (180 − 40) ÷ 2. However you dragged the apex, the two base-angle readouts never came apart: equal legs force equal base angles, at every apex angle, not just this one.
widget.criterionFeedback: The apex angle is what moves here — the criterion itself is not in question.
widget.angleFeedback: Bring the apex to 40° and read the base angles there.
widget.evidenceFeedback: Try the apex at a few different angles first — one drag is not evidence that the base angles always match.

predict.prompt: The apex is 40°. Each base angle will come out…

options.label: Bigger than 40° — they split the lion's share

predict.reveal: The apex takes only 40 of the triangle's 180 degrees, leaving 140 for the two base angles to split equally — 70 each, well above the apex. Equal legs force equal base angles, but nothing forces them to match the apex.

explanationVariants: Draw the bisector of the apex angle. It splits the triangle into two triangles sharing that bisector, with equal legs and equal half-angles — congruent by SAS. CPCTC then makes the base angles equal.
The apex-angle bisector creates two SAS-congruent triangles (equal legs, equal half-angles, shared bisector); their base angles correspond, so they're equal.

widget.prompt: What construction proves the base angles equal?

options.label: Bisect the apex angle, creating two triangles congruent by SAS
options.feedback: The bisector gives equal half-angles, the legs are equal, and the bisector is shared — SAS congruence, then CPCTC equates the base angles.

options.label: Measure both base angles with a protractor
options.feedback: Measuring checks one triangle, not all — the theorem needs a proof. The apex bisector gives SAS congruence.

options.label: Draw a circle through all three vertices
options.feedback: A circumscribed circle doesn't directly equate the base angles. The apex-angle bisector and SAS do.

options.label: Assume the base angles are equal
options.feedback: Assuming the conclusion is circular. The bisector-plus-SAS argument derives it.

steps.body: The bisector does triple duty. In an isosceles triangle, the segment from the apex is at once the **angle bisector**, the **perpendicular bisector of the base**, the **median**, and the **altitude** — all the same line. That coincidence is special to isosceles (and equilateral) triangles.

widget.prompt: In an isosceles triangle, the segment from the apex to the base midpoint is NOT which of these?

options.label: a side of the triangle
options.feedback: It's an interior segment — the altitude/median/bisector — not one of the triangle's three sides.

options.label: the altitude to the base
options.feedback: It IS the altitude — it meets the base at a right angle. So this can't be the 'not' answer.

options.label: the median to the base
options.feedback: It IS the median — it hits the base's midpoint. So this isn't the exception.

options.label: the apex angle bisector
options.feedback: It IS the angle bisector — it splits the apex angle in half. Not the exception.

explanationVariants: Two base angles of 65° use 130°, leaving 180 − 130 = 50° for the apex.

widget.prompt: An isosceles triangle has base angles of 65° each. What is its apex angle, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 65° is a BASE angle. The apex is what's left after both base angles: 180 − 65 − 65 = 50°.
115 = 180 − 65 subtracts only ONE base angle. Subtract both: 180 − 130 = 50°.

steps.body: Equal legs guarantee equal base angles — a one-way street for now. The reverse question (do equal base angles guarantee equal legs?) is the CONVERSE, and it deserves its own proof. That's the next lesson. For now: whenever you see two equal sides, you may immediately mark the base angles equal.

widget.prompt: You're told a triangle has two equal sides. What may you immediately conclude?

options.label: The angles opposite those sides are equal
options.feedback: Equal sides (legs) ⇒ equal opposite (base) angles, by the Base Angles Theorem.

options.label: All three angles are equal
options.feedback: Only the two BASE angles are forced equal — the apex can differ. All-equal happens only for equilateral.

options.label: The triangle is right-angled
options.feedback: Isosceles triangles needn't be right — the theorem is only about the two base angles being equal.

options.label: Nothing without more information
options.feedback: Equal sides are enough: the Base Angles Theorem immediately gives equal base angles.

hints: The two base angles are equal — set their expressions equal or use the angle sum.
Apex is 50°, so the two base angles share 180 − 50 = 130°.
explanationVariants: The apex is 50°, so the base angles share 180 − 50 = 130°, and being equal, each is 65°.

widget.prompt: An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 50°. One base angle is labeled (5x)°. Find x.

commonErrors.feedback: 65 is the base ANGLE in degrees, not x. Since 5x = 65, divide: x = 13.
10 would make 5x = 50, the APEX angle — but 5x is a BASE angle = 65, so x = 13.

takeaways: Base Angles Theorem: equal legs ⇒ equal base angles (opposite those legs).
Proof: bisect the apex angle → two SAS-congruent triangles → CPCTC.
The apex segment is bisector, median, altitude, and perpendicular bisector all at once.
steps.teaser: Next: run the theorem backward — equal base angles prove the triangle isosceles.
